subject: science
title: Chemistry — Chemical reactions
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Chemistry — Chemical reactions, KS3 Science (National Curriculum).
meta_desc: KS3 Science practice covering Chemistry — Chemical reactions, from the National Curriculum programme of study.
final_note: You worked through Chemistry — Chemical reactions: 8 programme-of-study statements.

concepts.def: A change in which new substances are made. The atoms in the starting substances separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways. No atom is made, destroyed or changed into a different kind of atom.
concepts.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms

concepts.def: Reactants are the substances you start with in a reaction. Products are the new substances made. Products have different properties from the reactants.
concepts.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms

concepts.def: A change in which no new substance is made, such as melting, boiling, condensing or dissolving. The particles stay the same; only their arrangement or spacing changes, and the change can usually be reversed.
concepts.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms

concepts.def: Clues that a new substance may have formed: a gas given off that was not there before, a new solid appearing, a lasting colour change, or the mixture getting hot or cold. They are clues, not proof: mixing paints changes colour and boiling makes bubbles without any new substance.
concepts.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms

concepts.def: A way of showing a reaction with the names of the substances: reactants on the left, products on the right, joined by an arrow that means 'reacts to make'. Example: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
concepts.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations

concepts.def: A way of showing a reaction with chemical formulae, for example 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. It shows which atoms are in each substance and how many of each substance react.
concepts.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations

concepts.def: A big number written in front of a formula in a symbol equation. It shows how many of that molecule (or unit) take part, and it multiplies every atom in the formula: 2H₂O means two water molecules, with 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms. A formula with no big number in front means one.
concepts.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations

concepts.def: A symbol equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, because atoms are not made or destroyed in a reaction. You balance an equation by changing the big numbers in front of formulae, never the small numbers inside a formula.
concepts.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations

concepts.def: Burning: a reaction of a substance with oxygen that transfers energy to the surroundings as heat and light. A fuel made of carbon and hydrogen (such as methane) burning in plenty of air makes carbon dioxide and water. A metal burns to make its oxide, for example magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. When oxygen is limited, some carbon monoxide and soot (carbon) form instead.
concepts.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

concepts.def: A substance that is burned to transfer energy, such as methane, butane, petrol or wax. Its atoms are not destroyed when it burns: they end up in the gases made.
concepts.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

concepts.def: A reaction in which heating breaks one compound down into two or more simpler substances. Many metal carbonates do this: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide.
concepts.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

concepts.def: A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. Burning is fast oxidation; rusting is slow oxidation of iron, which needs both oxygen and water. Heating copper in air oxidises it to black copper oxide.
concepts.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

concepts.def: A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in its compound, pushing it out. Example: iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one.
concepts.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions

concepts.def: A substance that is neutralised by an alkali. Acids have a pH below 7 and turn blue litmus red. Examples: hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, nitric acid, citric acid (in lemons) and vinegar.
concepts.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions

concepts.def: A base that dissolves in water. An alkali neutralises an acid. Alkali solutions have a pH above 7 and turn red litmus blue. Example: sodium hydroxide solution. Alkalis can damage skin and eyes just as acids can.
concepts.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions

concepts.def: The reaction between an acid and an alkali (or another base). It makes new substances, a salt and water, and moves the pH towards 7. It is a reaction, so some acid is neutralised as soon as any alkali is added.
concepts.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions

concepts.def: A scale, usually 0 to 14, that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is. Below 7 is acidic (the lower the number, the more acidic), 7 is neutral, and above 7 is alkaline (the higher the number, the more alkaline).
concepts.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators

concepts.def: Neither acidic nor alkaline: pH 7. Pure water is neutral.
concepts.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators

concepts.def: A substance that changes colour depending on how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
concepts.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators

concepts.def: An indicator with a range of colours that shows the pH number: red or orange for acids (low pH), green for neutral (pH 7), blue or purple for alkalis (high pH). You find the pH by matching the colour to a chart.
concepts.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators

concepts.def: An indicator that only shows acid or alkali: litmus is red in acids and blue in alkalis. Blue litmus paper turns red in an acid; red litmus paper turns blue in an alkali. Neither changes in a neutral solution.
concepts.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators

concepts.def: A compound made, along with hydrogen or water, when an acid reacts with a metal or a base such as an alkali. Its name has two parts: the first usually comes from the metal, the second from the acid. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates and nitric acid makes nitrates. Sodium chloride (table salt) is just one salt.
concepts.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen

concepts.def: Many metals, such as magnesium and zinc, react with acids: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Bubbles of hydrogen fizz off and the metal is used up as its atoms go into the salt, which stays dissolved.
concepts.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen

concepts.def: Hold a lit splint at the mouth of a test tube of the gas. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.
concepts.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen

concepts.def: acid + alkali → salt + water. For example, hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water. If exactly enough sodium hydroxide is added to hydrochloric acid, the solution ends at pH 7; evaporating the water then leaves the salt.
concepts.specStatementText: reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water

concepts.def: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up. The same mass of catalyst is left at the end, so it can be used again. The reaction makes the same products, in the same amount, just faster. Enzymes are catalysts in living things.
concepts.specStatementText: what catalysts do

mcqs.q: In every chemical reaction, what happens to the atoms?
options: Some of them are used up and then destroyed
They are rearranged into new substances
Some change into atoms of other elements
They stay in the same molecules as before
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
mcqs.explain: Yes. The atoms separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways, making new substances. No atom is made, destroyed or changed.
rationales: You may have thought atoms get used up because reactants seem to disappear. In fact every atom is still there after the reaction, joined in a new substance.
Yes. The atoms separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways, making new substances. No atom is made, destroyed or changed.
You may have thought a reaction turns one kind of atom into another. In fact atoms never change in a chemical reaction; only the way they are joined changes.
You may have thought the molecules just mix or stick together. In fact the atoms come apart and join up differently, so new molecules form.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows hydrogen reacting with chlorine. Which statement about the reaction is correct?
options: The same atoms are joined in a new way
The atoms have changed into new atoms
Some of the atoms have been used up
The two molecules have just mixed
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
mcqs.explain: Yes. Count them: 2 hydrogen and 2 chlorine atoms before, and 2 of each after. The atoms have separated and joined up differently, making hydrogen chloride.
rationales: Yes. Count them: 2 hydrogen and 2 chlorine atoms before, and 2 of each after. The atoms have separated and joined up differently, making hydrogen chloride.
You may have thought a reaction turns atoms into new kinds of atom. In fact the diagram shows the same hydrogen and chlorine atoms after the reaction, joined in a new way.
You may have thought atoms are used up in a reaction. In fact there are 2 hydrogen and 2 chlorine atoms both before and after; none has gone.
You may have thought the molecules stay whole and simply mix. In fact the H₂ and Cl₂ molecules have come apart, and new HCl molecules have formed.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the particles before and after some water is heated. Which statement is correct?
options: A gas forms, so it is a chemical reaction
The water has split into hydrogen and oxygen
No new substance forms: not a reaction
Some of the water is used up and destroyed
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
mcqs.explain: Yes. The water molecules are the same before and after; they have only moved far apart as the water boils. That is a change of state, not a chemical reaction.
rationales: You may have thought any change from liquid to gas is a reaction. In fact the molecules in the gas are the same water molecules, so no new substance has formed.
You may have thought heating splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. In fact each particle in the after box is still a whole water molecule.
Yes. The water molecules are the same before and after; they have only moved far apart as the water boils. That is a change of state, not a chemical reaction.
You may have thought the water is used up when it boils away. In fact all eight water molecules are still there, just spread out as a gas.

mcqs.q: Which of these changes is a chemical reaction?
options: Chocolate melting in the sun
Sugar dissolving in hot tea
Mixing two paints to make green
Wood burning on a bonfire
mcqs.specStatementText: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
mcqs.explain: Yes. Burning wood makes new substances, such as carbon dioxide, water and ash, that were not there before. It cannot be reversed.
rationales: You may have thought melting makes a new substance because the chocolate looks different. In fact melting is a change of state: the chocolate sets again when it cools.
You may have thought the sugar turns into something new because it disappears. In fact the sugar is still there, spread out in the tea, and evaporating the water would leave it.
You may have thought a colour change always means a reaction. In fact the blue and yellow paint particles are just mixed; no new substance forms.
Yes. Burning wood makes new substances, such as carbon dioxide, water and ash, that were not there before. It cannot be reversed.

mcqs.q: Iron reacts with sulfur to make a single product. Which word equation is correct?
options: iron + sulfur → iron sulfate
iron + sulfur → iron sulfide
iron sulfide → iron + sulfur
iron + sulfur = iron sulfide
mcqs.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
mcqs.explain: Yes. Iron and sulfur join to make iron sulfide. The reactants go on the left, the product on the right, and the arrow means 'reacts to make'.
rationales: You may have mixed up -ide and -ate. A sulfate also contains oxygen, but only iron and sulfur reacted, so the product is iron sulfide.
Yes. Iron and sulfur join to make iron sulfide. The reactants go on the left, the product on the right, and the arrow means 'reacts to make'.
You may have put the product on the left. Reactants go on the left of the arrow and products on the right; iron and sulfur are what you start with.
You may have thought the arrow means 'equals'. In fact it means 'reacts to make': iron sulfide is a new substance, not the same as iron and sulfur.

mcqs.q: Magnesium (Mg) burns in oxygen (O₂) to make magnesium oxide (MgO). Which symbol equation is balanced and correct?
options: 2Mg + O₂ → Mg₂O₂
Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
Mg + O₂ → MgO + O
mcqs.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
mcqs.explain: Yes. Left: 2 Mg and 2 O. Right: 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O. The formulae are unchanged and every atom balances.
rationales: You may have changed the small numbers to make it balance. The formula of magnesium oxide is MgO and must not change; balance with big numbers in front instead.
You may have balanced the oxygen and stopped. Check every atom: the right now has 2 Mg but the left has 1, so you also need 2Mg.
Yes. Left: 2 Mg and 2 O. Right: 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O. The formulae are unchanged and every atom balances.
You may have written the spare oxygen atom as a product. A lone oxygen atom is not made; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO puts both oxygen atoms into magnesium oxide.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows hydrogen reacting with oxygen to make water. Which symbol equation matches the diagram?
options: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂
H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
2H + O → H₂O
mcqs.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
mcqs.explain: Yes. The diagram shows two H₂ molecules and one O₂ molecule making two H₂O molecules: 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms on each side.
rationales: Yes. The diagram shows two H₂ molecules and one O₂ molecule making two H₂O molecules: 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms on each side.
You may have joined the two formulae to make the atoms match. In fact the product is water, H₂O: the diagram shows two separate H₂O molecules, not one H₂O₂ particle.
You may have written the substances without counting atoms. This has 2 O on the left but 1 O on the right, and the diagram shows two water molecules.
You may have thought hydrogen and oxygen gases are single atoms. The diagram shows them as pairs, so their formulae are H₂ and O₂.

mcqs.q: How many oxygen atoms are on each side of this equation? CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
options: Left 2, right 3
Left 4, right 3
Left 4, right 2
Left 4, right 4
mcqs.specStatementText: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
mcqs.explain: Yes. 2O₂ has 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms. On the right, CO₂ has 2 and 2H₂O has 2 × 1 = 2, so 4 in total.
mcqs.working: Left: 2O₂ = 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms. Right: CO₂ has 2 oxygen atoms, and 2H₂O = 2 × 1 = 2 oxygen atoms, so 2 + 2 = 4. Left 4, right 4: oxygen is balanced.
rationales: You may have ignored the big numbers. 2O₂ means two O₂ molecules (4 O), and 2H₂O means two water molecules (2 O), so it is 4 on each side.
You may have doubled only the first symbol in 2H₂O. The big 2 doubles the whole molecule, so 2H₂O has 2 oxygen atoms and the right has 2 + 2 = 4.
You may have counted the O in H₂O as no atoms because it has no small number. It stands for one atom, so 2H₂O has 2 oxygen atoms and the right has 4.
Yes. 2O₂ has 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms. On the right, CO₂ has 2 and 2H₂O has 2 × 1 = 2, so 4 in total.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows methane burning in plenty of oxygen. Where do the hydrogen atoms from the methane end up?
options: In hydrogen gas molecules
In the water molecules made
Turned into heat and light
Destroyed by the flame
mcqs.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Each hydrogen atom joins with oxygen: the four hydrogen atoms end up in two water molecules, H₂O. Complete burning makes carbon dioxide and water.
rationales: You may have thought the hydrogen is released as hydrogen gas. In fact it joins with oxygen: the diagram shows the hydrogen atoms in water molecules.
Yes. Each hydrogen atom joins with oxygen: the four hydrogen atoms end up in two water molecules, H₂O. Complete burning makes carbon dioxide and water.
You may have thought part of the fuel turns into energy. In fact every atom is still there after burning; energy is transferred, but atoms do not become energy.
You may have thought burning destroys the fuel. In fact all four hydrogen atoms are still there after the reaction, joined to oxygen atoms.

mcqs.q: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame. Which substance is made?
options: Soot made of carbon
Carbon dioxide and water
Nothing: it burns away
Solid magnesium oxide
mcqs.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. A metal burns by joining with oxygen to make its oxide: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, a white powder.
rationales: You may have thought burning always leaves soot. Soot is carbon, and magnesium contains no carbon, so the product is magnesium oxide, a white powder.
You may have used the equation for burning fuels. Carbon dioxide and water need carbon and hydrogen, which magnesium does not contain; it makes magnesium oxide.
You may have thought the magnesium is destroyed as it burns. In fact its atoms join with oxygen to make magnesium oxide, which weighs more than the magnesium did.
Yes. A metal burns by joining with oxygen to make its oxide: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, a white powder.

mcqs.q: Calcium carbonate is heated strongly. What does it form?
options: Calcium, carbon and oxygen gas
Water and carbon dioxide gas
Calcium oxide and carbon dioxide
Only melted calcium carbonate
mcqs.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. This is thermal decomposition: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. Many metal carbonates break down like this to a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
rationales: You may have thought decomposition splits a compound into its elements. In fact it gives simpler compounds: calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
You may have used the equation for burning a fuel. Calcium carbonate contains no hydrogen, so no water can form; it gives calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
Yes. This is thermal decomposition: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. Many metal carbonates break down like this to a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
You may have thought heating only melts a solid. In fact strong heating breaks calcium carbonate down into new substances.

mcqs.q: Copper is heated in a hot, blue Bunsen flame. Its surface turns black. What is the black layer?
options: Copper oxide, as oxygen joined the copper
Soot (carbon) left on it by the flame
Copper changed by heat, with nothing added
Copper that has turned into carbon
mcqs.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Copper reacts with oxygen from the air to make black copper oxide. Gaining oxygen like this is oxidation.
rationales: Yes. Copper reacts with oxygen from the air to make black copper oxide. Gaining oxygen like this is oxidation.
You may have thought heating in a flame always leaves soot. A hot, blue flame does not make soot; the black layer is copper oxide.
You may have thought heat alone changed the copper. In fact oxygen from the air joined on, making a new substance, copper oxide.
You may have thought one element can turn into another. Copper atoms cannot become carbon atoms; the copper has joined with oxygen.

mcqs.q: An iron nail rusts in damp air. None of the rust flakes off. What happens to the mass of the nail and its rust?
options: It goes down, as rust eats away the iron
It stays the same, as rust was already there
It stays the same, as air has no mass
It goes up, as oxygen from the air joins on
mcqs.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Rusting is oxidation: oxygen (and water) from the air join the iron to make rust. Their mass is added, so the mass goes up.
rationales: You may have thought rust eats the iron away. In fact the iron atoms are all still there, in the rust; oxygen and water have been added, so the mass goes up.
You may have thought the rust was hidden in the nail. In fact rust is a new substance made with oxygen and water from the air, so the mass goes up.
You may have thought gases cannot add mass. In fact oxygen has mass, and the oxygen that joins the iron adds to the mass.
Yes. Rusting is oxidation: oxygen (and water) from the air join the iron to make rust. Their mass is added, so the mass goes up.

mcqs.q: Iron is more reactive than copper. An iron nail is left in blue copper sulfate solution. A brown coating forms. What is it?
options: Iron that has changed into copper
Rust, because the iron nail is wet
Copper, pushed out of the copper sulfate
Copper sulfate that has stuck to the nail
mcqs.specStatementText: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. This is displacement: the more reactive iron takes copper's place, making iron sulfate and copper. The copper forms the coating.
rationales: You may have thought the iron turns into copper. Atoms cannot change element; the copper atoms came from the copper sulfate.
You may have matched the brown colour to rust. In fact iron displaces copper from the solution, and the coating is copper.
Yes. This is displacement: the more reactive iron takes copper's place, making iron sulfate and copper. The copper forms the coating.
You may have thought the substances stay the same and just stick together. In fact a reaction happens: the coating is copper metal, and the blue colour fades.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true of every acid?
options: It eats away any material it touches
It can be neutralised by an alkali
It has the same pH as all other acids
It bubbles and fizzes on its own
mcqs.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Every acid reacts with an alkali and is neutralised, making a salt and water. That is how acids and alkalis are defined.
rationales: You may have thought every acid burns and eats things away. Many acids, such as citric acid in lemons, do not; what every acid does is react with an alkali.
Yes. Every acid reacts with an alkali and is neutralised, making a salt and water. That is how acids and alkalis are defined.
You may have thought pH only shows acid or alkali. In fact acids have different pH values, from 0 up to just below 7.
You may have thought fizzing is part of being an acid. An acid on its own does not fizz; bubbles appear only when it reacts with something.

mcqs.q: A substance dissolves in water. Which result shows that the substance is an alkali?
options: It neutralises acids
It turns blue litmus red
It has a pH below 7
It reacts with nothing
mcqs.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. A substance that dissolves in water and neutralises acids is a base that dissolves: an alkali. Its solution also has a pH above 7.
rationales: Yes. A substance that dissolves in water and neutralises acids is a base that dissolves: an alkali. Its solution also has a pH above 7.
You may have mixed up the litmus colours. Turning blue litmus red shows an acid; an alkali turns red litmus blue.
You may have thought the pH scale runs the other way. Below 7 is acidic; an alkali has a pH above 7.
You may have thought alkalis are harmless and do nothing. In fact alkalis react with acids, and can damage skin and eyes.

mcqs.q: When an alkali neutralises an acid, what happens to the acid?
options: It breaks down on its own and stops being acid
It reacts with the alkali to make a salt
It is simply stopped from burning anything
It is only diluted by the water in the alkali
mcqs.specStatementText: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
mcqs.explain: Yes. Neutralisation is a reaction between the acid and the alkali. It makes a salt and water.
rationales: You may have thought neutralisation is the acid breaking down. In fact the acid reacts with the alkali; both are used up and a salt and water form.
Yes. Neutralisation is a reaction between the acid and the alkali. It makes a salt and water.
You may have thought an alkali only stops the acid working. In fact the alkali reacts with the acid; it is not a shield.
You may have thought the alkali just waters the acid down. Diluting does not neutralise an acid; the alkali reacts with it.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?
options: Higher numbers are more acidic
Neutral solutions have a pH of 0
Lower numbers are more acidic
All acids have exactly the same pH
mcqs.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
mcqs.explain: Yes. The lower the pH below 7, the more acidic the solution. pH 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.
rationales: You may have thought a bigger number means more acid. In fact higher numbers are more alkaline; pH 1 is far more acidic than pH 5.
You may have thought 'no acid' belongs at zero. Neutral is pH 7, in the middle; pH 0 is extremely acidic.
Yes. The lower the pH below 7, the more acidic the solution. pH 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.
You may have thought pH only tells you acid or alkali. Acids have different pH values: the lower the number, the more acidic.

mcqs.q: Universal indicator is green at pH 7, blue at pH 9 and purple at pH 13. A cleaner turns it blue. What does this show?
options: It is more alkaline than purple liquids
It is as alkaline as a purple liquid
It is harmless, as it is not acidic
It is less alkaline than a purple liquid
mcqs.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
mcqs.explain: Yes. Blue means about pH 9, which is alkaline but less alkaline than pH 13 (purple). The higher the pH above 7, the more alkaline.
rationales: You may have thought a lower pH number means more alkaline. In fact pH 13 (purple) is more alkaline than pH 9 (blue).
You may have thought indicator colours only show acid or alkali. Universal indicator also shows how alkaline: purple (pH 13) is more alkaline than blue (pH 9).
You may have thought alkalis are harmless. In fact alkaline cleaners can damage skin and eyes; the colour shows a pH of about 9.
Yes. Blue means about pH 9, which is alkaline but less alkaline than pH 13 (purple). The higher the pH above 7, the more alkaline.

mcqs.q: Blue litmus paper is dipped into a solution and stays blue. What does this show?
options: It is not acidic, as an acid turns it red
It is alkaline, as blue means alkali
It is acidic, as acids turn litmus blue
It is neutral, as nothing changed
mcqs.specStatementText: the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
mcqs.explain: Yes. Acids turn blue litmus red. Blue litmus stays blue in both neutral and alkaline solutions, so you only know the solution is not acidic.
rationales: Yes. Acids turn blue litmus red. Blue litmus stays blue in both neutral and alkaline solutions, so you only know the solution is not acidic.
You may have thought blue litmus staying blue proves an alkali. Blue litmus was blue to start with, and stays blue in neutral solutions too.
You may have swapped the litmus colours. Litmus is red in acids, so an acid would have turned the blue paper red.
You may have thought no colour change means neutral. Blue litmus also stays blue in an alkali, so the solution could be neutral or alkaline.

mcqs.q: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid. One product is zinc chloride. What is the other product?
options: Water, which stays in the beaker
Hydrogen gas, which fizzes off
Oxygen gas, which fizzes off
Zinc oxide, a white solid
mcqs.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
mcqs.explain: Yes. metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. The salt here is zinc chloride, and the bubbles of gas are hydrogen.
rationales: You may have mixed this up with neutralisation. Acid + alkali gives a salt and water, but metal + acid gives a salt and hydrogen.
Yes. metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. The salt here is zinc chloride, and the bubbles of gas are hydrogen.
You may have thought the bubbles are oxygen. A metal and an acid make hydrogen, which burns with a squeaky pop.
You may have thought a metal always makes its oxide. No oxygen gas is used here; the zinc ends up in the salt, and the other product is hydrogen.

mcqs.q: Magnesium reacts with sulfuric acid. Which salt is made?
options: Sodium chloride
Magnesium acid
Magnesium chloride
Magnesium sulfate
mcqs.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
mcqs.explain: Yes. Sulfuric acid makes sulfates, and the first part of the name comes from the metal: magnesium sulfate.
rationales: You may have thought 'salt' means table salt. There is no sodium or chlorine here; the salt is magnesium sulfate.
You may have kept the word acid in the name. The acid has reacted, so the salt is named with -sulfate: magnesium sulfate.
You may have thought every salt is a chloride. Chlorides come from hydrochloric acid; sulfuric acid makes sulfates.
Yes. Sulfuric acid makes sulfates, and the first part of the name comes from the metal: magnesium sulfate.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is added to hydrochloric acid and it fizzes. Which test shows that the gas is hydrogen?
options: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
A glowing splint bursts into flame
It turns clear limewater milky
It turns damp blue litmus red
mcqs.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
mcqs.explain: Yes. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lit splint is held at the mouth of the tube.
rationales: Yes. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lit splint is held at the mouth of the tube.
You may have thought the gas is oxygen. A glowing splint relighting is the test for oxygen; metal + acid makes hydrogen.
You may have thought any fizzing gas is carbon dioxide. There is no carbon in magnesium or hydrochloric acid, so the gas is hydrogen.
You may have thought the gas is acidic because it comes from the acid. In fact hydrogen is not an acid and does not turn litmus red; the test for it is a lit splint.

mcqs.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to hydrochloric acid. It fizzes and slowly disappears. Where has the magnesium gone?
options: It has been eaten away to nothing by the acid
It has changed into the bubbles of hydrogen
It is now in magnesium chloride, in solution
It is still magnesium, just mixed into the acid
mcqs.specStatementText: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
mcqs.explain: Yes. The magnesium atoms are in the salt, magnesium chloride, which stays dissolved in the solution. Evaporating the water would leave it.
rationales: You may have thought acids just eat metals away. In fact the magnesium atoms are all still there, in the salt magnesium chloride.
You may have thought the metal turns into the gas. Magnesium atoms cannot become hydrogen; the hydrogen comes from the acid.
Yes. The magnesium atoms are in the salt, magnesium chloride, which stays dissolved in the solution. Evaporating the water would leave it.
You may have thought the magnesium just dissolves unchanged. In fact it has reacted: it is now part of a new substance, magnesium chloride.

mcqs.q: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, an alkali. What are the products?
options: Sodium chloride and water
Sodium chloride and hydrogen
Only the acid, now diluted
Nothing, as they cancel out
mcqs.specStatementText: reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
mcqs.explain: Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, so the salt is sodium chloride.
rationales: Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, so the salt is sodium chloride.
You may have mixed this up with acid + metal. An acid and an alkali make a salt and water, not hydrogen.
You may have thought the alkali just waters the acid down. In fact the acid reacts with the alkali, making sodium chloride and water.
You may have thought the acid and alkali cancel each other out to nothing. In fact their atoms make new substances: sodium chloride and water.

mcqs.q: The graph shows the pH as an alkali is slowly added to an acid. Which statement is correct when 20 cm³ of alkali has been added?
options: No acid has reacted, as the pH is not 7
It is more acidic than it was at the start
Some acid and alkali have turned into nothing
Some of the acid has been neutralised
mcqs.specStatementText: reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
mcqs.explain: Yes. Each drop of alkali reacts with some acid, so the pH has risen from 1 to about 2. It reaches 7 only when all the acid has reacted.
rationales: You may have thought neutralisation only happens at pH 7. In fact the alkali reacts as soon as it is added; the pH reaches 7 only when all the acid is used up.
You may have thought a higher pH means more acidic. The pH has risen from 1 to about 2, so the mixture is less acidic than at the start.
You may have thought the acid and alkali cancel out to nothing. In fact their atoms are still there, in the salt and water made.
Yes. Each drop of alkali reacts with some acid, so the pH has risen from 1 to about 2. It reaches 7 only when all the acid has reacted.

figure.alt: A line graph. The horizontal axis is labelled volume of alkali added (cm³), with marks at 0, 10, 20 and 30. The vertical axis is labelled pH, with marks at 0, 7 and 14, and a dashed line across at pH 7. The line starts at pH 1 at 0 cm³ and rises slowly to about pH 2 at 20 cm³. Near 25 cm³ it rises very steeply through pH 7, then levels off at about pH 12 by 30 cm³.

mcqs.q: Alkali is added to an acid until the pH is exactly 7. The water is then evaporated. What is left?
options: Nothing, as they cancel out
A salt formed by the reaction
The acid and alkali, unchanged
The alkali, as the acid broke down
mcqs.specStatementText: reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
mcqs.explain: Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. When the water is evaporated, the solid salt is left behind.
rationales: You may have thought the acid and alkali cancel to nothing. In fact they react to make a salt and water, and the salt is left when the water evaporates.
Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. When the water is evaporated, the solid salt is left behind.
You may have thought the acid and alkali just mix. In fact they react, so neither is left at pH 7; a new substance, a salt, is left.
You may have thought neutralisation is the acid breaking down alone. In fact the acid and the alkali both react, making a salt and water.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?
options: It speeds up a reaction but is used up
It makes a reaction give more product
It speeds up a reaction and is not used up
It changes which products are made
mcqs.specStatementText: what catalysts do
mcqs.explain: Yes. A catalyst makes a reaction go faster and is left over unchanged at the end, so it can be used again.
rationales: You may have thought a catalyst is used up like a reactant. In fact the same mass of catalyst is left at the end.
You may have thought a catalyst gives more product. In fact it gives the same amount of product, just faster.
Yes. A catalyst makes a reaction go faster and is left over unchanged at the end, so it can be used again.
You may have thought a catalyst changes the products. In fact the same reaction happens, making the same products, only faster.

mcqs.q: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Afterwards, any solid left is filtered off and dried, with none spilled. How does its mass compare with the start?
options: It is the same as at the start
It is less, as some was used up
It is zero, as it became the oxygen
It is more, as it took in oxygen
mcqs.specStatementText: what catalysts do
mcqs.explain: Yes. Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst: it speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so the same mass is recovered.
rationales: Yes. Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst: it speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so the same mass is recovered.
You may have thought a catalyst is used up. In fact all of it is recovered unchanged at the end.
You may have thought the oxygen comes from the catalyst. The oxygen comes from the hydrogen peroxide; the manganese(IV) oxide is all still there.
You may have thought the catalyst joins with the products. In fact it is left over unchanged, so its mass is the same.

mcqs.q: The graph shows the volume of gas made by the same reaction with and without a catalyst. What did the catalyst change?
options: The total volume of gas made
Only how fast the gas was made
Which gas the reaction made
Whether any gas was made at all
mcqs.specStatementText: what catalysts do
mcqs.explain: Yes. Both lines level off at 50 cm³, so the same amount of gas was made; the catalyst only made it faster.
rationales: You may have thought a catalyst gives more product. Both lines end at 50 cm³, so the total is the same.
Yes. Both lines level off at 50 cm³, so the same amount of gas was made; the catalyst only made it faster.
You may have thought a catalyst changes the products. It speeds up the same reaction, which makes the same gas.
You may have thought the reaction needs the catalyst to happen. The dashed line shows gas being made without it, only more slowly.

figure.alt: A line graph. The horizontal axis is labelled time (s), with marks at 0, 100 and 200. The vertical axis is labelled volume of gas (cm³), with marks at 0, 25 and 50. A solid line labelled with catalyst rises steeply and levels off at 50 cm³ after about 60 s. A dashed line labelled without catalyst rises more slowly and levels off at the same height, 50 cm³, after about 150 s.

specSource: National Curriculum in England, key stage 3 science — Chemistry; Chemistry — Chemical reactions (DfE 2013 programme of study, verbatim)

specStatements.text: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water

scopeNotes.decision: A chemical reaction is tested as the rearrangement of atoms into new substances, with no atom made, destroyed or changed into another element; reactions are told apart from physical changes (changes of state, dissolving, mixing) by whether a new substance forms.
scopeNotes.basis: The programme of study names 'chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms'. Energy changes in reactions are a separate key stage 3 heading (Energetics), and bond breaking and making as an energy account is GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or rationale uses bond energies or energy values. Every particle diagram shows the same atoms before and after, joined or not joined.

scopeNotes.decision: Word equations are written and read; symbol equations are read by counting the atoms of each element on each side, and simple ones are balanced with given formulae using single-digit balancing numbers.
scopeNotes.basis: Working out formulae from ion charges or valency, ionic equations and state symbols are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every formula needed is given in the item, its stem or its diagram; balancing numbers are single digits; no equation contains brackets, ions or state symbols, and no item asks the student to work out a formula from ion charges or valency.

scopeNotes.decision: Combustion (fuels of carbon and hydrogen burning to carbon dioxide and water; metals burning to oxides), thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide, oxidation as gain of oxygen, and displacement of a less reactive metal from its compound by a more reactive one.
scopeNotes.basis: Oxidation and reduction as electron transfer, and the chemistry of incomplete combustion beyond 'carbon monoxide and soot form when oxygen is limited', are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015). The reactivity series itself belongs to the key stage 3 heading 'Materials'.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or rationale describes oxidation in terms of electrons. Carbon monoxide appears only in the combustion concept card; soot appears in items only as the wrong idea that burning leaves soot. The displacement item states in its stem which metal is more reactive.

scopeNotes.decision: An acid is a substance that is neutralised by an alkali, and an alkali (a base that dissolves in water) is a substance that neutralises an acid; neutralisation is a reaction that makes new substances.
scopeNotes.basis: Explanations of acids and alkalis in terms of hydrogen and hydroxide ions, Brønsted–Lowry theory, and the difference between strong and weak acids are GCSE or A-level content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or rationale mentions ions or proton transfer, and none mentions strong or weak acids.

scopeNotes.decision: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic (lower is more acidic), 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline (higher is more alkaline); universal indicator shows the pH by its colour, and litmus only shows acid (red) or alkali (blue).
scopeNotes.basis: pH as a measure of hydrogen ion concentration, its logarithmic scale and pH calculations are GCSE or A-level content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Indicator colours are those in the site's lesson (red or orange for acids, green for neutral, blue or purple for alkalis; litmus red in acids and blue in alkalis); where an item needs exact colour and pH pairs, the stem gives them. No item asks for a pH calculation.

scopeNotes.decision: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint; salts made from hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acids are chlorides, sulfates and nitrates.
scopeNotes.basis: The programme of study lists reactions of acids with metals and with alkalis but not with carbonates, so acid + carbonate is not tested here. Ionic equations and electron transfer in these reactions are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks about an acid reacting with a carbonate; limewater appears only in a wrong option about the gas made by magnesium and acid. Only metals that react readily with dilute acids (magnesium and zinc) are used.

scopeNotes.decision: Acid + alkali → salt + water; the pH moves towards 7 as an alkali is added, and some acid is neutralised before the pH reaches 7; evaporating the water leaves the salt.
scopeNotes.basis: The ionic equation for neutralisation, titration calculations and the interpretation of pH curves are GCSE or A-level content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: One item shows a pH graph, but the student only reads the pH at a given volume and compares it with the start; no item uses ions or asks for a calculation.

scopeNotes.decision: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up (the same mass is left at the end); the same reaction happens, making the same products in the same amount.
scopeNotes.basis: Activation energy and reaction profiles are GCSE content (DfE, GCSE combined science subject content, 2015); how enzymes work is not part of this heading.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or rationale mentions activation energy or reaction profiles; enzymes appear only in the catalyst concept card, by name.
